summary: A 1970 note on protocols and data formats from two RAND authors. It updates RFC 66, was updated by RFC 93, and was replaced by RFC 123.

plainLanguage.summary: RFC 80 discusses an early ARPANET connection setup and tools for adapting programs to network data formats. It presents proposals and asks for feedback.

questions: what is the initial connection protocol
what did rfc 80 propose for initial connections
subtitle: Discusses early connection setup and adaptable ways to handle protocols and data formats.

tldr.problem: The note discusses an error in the illustrated Initial Connection Protocol and the difficulty of adapting existing programs to network formats.
tldr.mechanism: It restates the RFC 66 sequence, proposes a variant using two fewer network messages, and describes a Form Machine and Protocol Manager.
tldr.outcome: RFC 80 was updated by RFC 93 and obsoleted by RFC 123; it is a historical discussion note.

today: RFC 80 was updated by RFC 93 and obsoleted by RFC 123. It is a historical discussion of ARPANET protocols and data formats.

sections.title: Restating the Initial Connection Protocol
sections.content:
The note identifies a problem in the diagram of the Initial Connection Protocol in RFC 66: both server and user send all messages before the connection is established, contrary to Network Document No. 1. It restates the sequence and proposes making the server process name a parameter, with zero as the special value for loggers.

A variation deletes two steps. The user listens on its sockets for calls from the server, reducing network messages by two and sending server socket information only once.
sections.plainLanguage: The note corrects the order in an earlier connection sequence. It also proposes a shorter variant that removes two network messages.

sections.title: Adapting Data Formats
sections.content:
The authors argue that network hosts must support existing programs and terminals that were not designed for network use. They describe a Form Machine, an experimental package that applies compiled descriptions of data formats to incoming and outgoing data streams.

The described features include character-code translation, insertion of literals, skipping strings, record sequence number generation, string-length computation, concatenation of messages and field transposition.
sections.plainLanguage: The proposed Form Machine translates or reshapes data according to a stored format description. That lets different programs exchange data without each being rebuilt for the network.

sections.title: Managing Protocol Sequences
sections.content:
The Network Services Program lets users work directly with NCP commands such as LISTEN and INIT. The note says repeated manual handshaking is laborious for researchers who often use the same remote program.

A planned Protocol Manager would let users define, store, retrieve and execute prepared command sequences. A sequence could include pause points for user input or parameters supplied by the remote party.
sections.plainLanguage: The Protocol Manager would save and replay a sequence of network commands. It could pause when a user or remote host needs to supply a value.
